title: How IRCTC survives the Tatkal rush

scenes.text: Tatkal opens at ten, and it feels like all of India hits Book at once. How does IRCTC keep up?
Welcome to How It Scales, by Curiously.
In May 2025, IRCTC booked a record nearly thirty-two thousand tickets in one minute.
Let's follow one booking, from tap to ticket.
Step one, getting in. Up to half the login attempts at Tatkal's opening were bots. Most are now blocked, the Railways says.
Online Tatkal now needs an Aadhaar-verified account, and authorised agents can't book in the first half hour.
Step two, you search. The trains, the seats left. That's reading. Nothing changes.
Step three, you hit Book. That's writing. It takes a seat away, and no two people can get the same one.
Reading can be copied. Writing can't.
So the page's unchanging parts, like the logo and buttons, are copied onto servers near you. That's a content delivery network.
Most of IRCTC's unchanging content now comes from those copies, the Railways says.
Your booking goes to the Railways' one connected reservation system, which station counters and agents use too.
Today's system handles about thirty-two thousand bookings a minute, the Railways says. That record came very close.
So trains are moving to a new system, designed for over forty lakh enquiries a minute and over one and a half lakh bookings. Far more room for reading than writing.
So at ten, most bots are kept out, copies carry what never changes, and IRCTC's servers keep their strength for the one thing that can't be copied: your booking.
